items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left, and on the right <radical>two</radical> bars stacked over a line of <radical>ground</radical>, carried on a <radical>stick</radical> each and <radical>split</radical> apart at the foot into a pair of legs. It is a tray on a stand, lifted with both hands. He is not setting it down — he is holding it up for somebody above him to take, which is what it is to <radical>submit</radical> a thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> on top, and underneath it that little sealed <radical>cocoon</radical>, tucked well out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped itself up, went under the soil, and never came back out. You can dig the whole mound over and there is nothing left in there to find. It is <radical>gone</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tree</radical>: a <radical>stick</radical> straight up the middle, branches <radical>split</radical> away either side, and laid across the very top an extra <radical>lid</radical> of a stroke, drawn longer than the <radical>one</radical> below it. That top bar marks the last inch of the highest twig — as far up as this tree is ever going to go. The tip is the <radical>end</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Matsu is the woodsman who only ever takes the tip. He climbs the whole tree, snips the last bud off the top of it, and calls down 「<reading>まつ</reading>」 to say he has got there. まつ means there is nothing above him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> is pulled across the top of the sky, and a <radical>person</radical> slips underneath it just as the last of the <radical>evening</radical> drains away. Once that lid is on, nothing more gets in — no sun, no colour, nobody else. The lid down over the evening, with somebody still out under it: <radical>night</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ya is the yakitori man who only opens once the lid is down. The cart comes out of nowhere, the lantern goes up, and he calls one syllable into the dark — 「<reading>や</reading>」 — which is the entire advertisement. If you can hear や, it is night.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> is being driven up a track: the <radical>road</radical> sweeps in underneath it, the surface <radical>splits</radical> into ruts, and packed <radical>earth</radical> climbs the whole way up. It is a long haul and the flock keeps stopping dead. But the last one is over the top and into the pen, and the job is <radical>accomplished</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Tatsu is the drover who marks the top of every hill the same way: one slap on the gatepost and a barked 「<reading>たつ</reading>」 — done, next. He has said it at every gate between here and the coast. たつ means it is finished.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the bottom, and above her a <radical>broom</radical> held up on its <radical>stick</radical>, with a bar of <radical>ground</radical> ruled straight across the top. She is not sweeping out somebody else's household here. The broom, the floor and the roofline over both are hers, and the person who runs them is the <radical>wife</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.
